description: We are a multidisciplinary team bringing together medicine, engineering and programmation. We are passionate about building technology that protects human health, even beyond Earth.
summary:
CosmoTwin: the digital health software that travels with you when Earth is too far to answer.

On Mars, a message to mission control can take up to 22 minutes each way, so astronauts must make medical decisions on their own.

That is why CosmoTwin does not depend on a connection. It runs entirely on board, with no internet or link to Earth.

CosmoTwin is a digital twin of the astronaut, built as a web app. It turns sensor data into an animated companion that talks to them. It compares every reading with the astronaut’s own 14-day Earth baseline and predicts health trends 7 days ahead. When an alert appears, it switches to an autonomous mode with step-by-step guidance and a report. Apart from critical alerts, the astronaut decides what to share with the flight surgeon.

Two modes:

Inside the ship: it monitors the astronaut awake and asleep.
Outside the ship: during a spacewalk, it tracks vital signs and crew communication. We recreated the real 2013 EVA 23 water-in-helmet incident to show how early detection helps.

This is a working demo, a model of the full system. Covering everything was impossible, so it focuses on the main risks and alerts for astronaut health. Its modular design lets us add new ones.

Built on NASA standards (NASA-STD-3001) and the Human Research Program’s five spaceflight hazards, it keeps data private by default.
details:
CosmoTwin is a digital health twin for astronauts on long missions. Its core, and our main differentiator, is an offline medical triage chatbot. It runs on pre-loaded decision trees based on real medical diagnostic protocols and severity scales.

When a symptom or emergency appears, the astronaut, or a crewmate acting as a third party, answers a guided questionnaire in the chat. Each answer moves through the decision tree. The chatbot then:

  1. classifies the severity level,
  2. tells the crew exactly what to do now, step by step,
  3. says when and how to escalate to the flight surgeon,
  4. prepares a report ready to send when communication is available.

No connection is needed. The decision trees are stored on board, so triage works with no internet and no link to Earth. This matters because on Mars a message to mission control can take up to 22 minutes each way, and communications can fail completely.

Around the chatbot, CosmoTwin adds health monitoring that gives it context:

  • Sense. It reads pulse, HRV, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, exercise and radiation from wearable sensors and a dosimeter, plus a two-minute daily self-report. It can also estimate pulse from the camera using rPPG.
  • Compare and predict. It compares each reading with the astronaut’s own 14-day Earth baseline and projects trends 7 days ahead.
  • Act. When an alert appears, an autonomous mode guides a step-by-step protocol and shows how long mission control will take to answer.

It works in two modes:

  • Inside the spacecraft: it monitors the astronaut awake and asleep, with self-logging, monitoring and prediction views.
  • Outside the spacecraft (spacewalks): it tracks vital signs and crew communication. We recreated the real 2013 EVA 23 water-in-helmet incident to show why early detection matters.

A demo built to grow

This is a working demo, a model of the full system. Covering every possible condition was impossible in a hackathon, so we focused on the main health risks and alerts that affect astronauts, guided by NASA’s Human Research Program. The decision trees and indicators are modular, so new protocols, symptoms and alerts can be added without changing the core.

Benefits

  • Works without a connection. Triage, monitoring and protocols run fully on board.
  • Anyone on the crew can use it. A crewmate can fill in the questionnaire if the astronaut can’t.
  • Grounded in real medicine. Decision trees follow real diagnostic protocols, and thresholds come from NASA-STD-3001 and clinical guidelines. Each value shows its source.
  • Protects privacy and data integrity. Data stays on the device, and it is private by default. The astronaut chooses what to share with the flight surgeon, and only critical alerts are always sent.
  • Personalized. Comparing against each astronaut’s own baseline reduces false alarms.

Intended impact

To give crews reliable medical guidance that does not have to wait for Earth. The same approach can help Earth analogs with delayed or no access to a doctor: Antarctic bases, submarines, remote communities and patients on prolonged bed rest.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework, packaged as a single lightweight file that runs in the browser
  • Rule-based decision trees for the triage chatbot
  • SVG for the animated twin, charts and body map

How is it creative?

Instead of a cold dashboard, the astronaut talks to a version of themselves. The twin’s face reflects their health and the fluid shift of microgravity, it falls asleep at night, and its helmet fogs up during a spacewalk when suit humidity rises. The triage chat feels like a conversation but follows a strict medical decision tree behind the scenes.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delay and blackouts. This is why everything works offline.
  • Trust. Astronauts tend to hide symptoms so they won’t be grounded, so privacy is the default.
  • Stress in emergencies. Short, guided questions are easier than reading a manual.
  • Safety. It does not replace the flight surgeon, and it always says when to escalate.
  • Scope. We prioritized the main risks and built the system to be expanded.
  • Accessibility. Mobile support, accessible contrast, and Spanish and English.
